title: Precision Alignment: Adjustable Sutures in Strabismus Surgery
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the surgical techniques, patient selection, and post-operative refinement of ocular alignment using adjustable suture methods. Designed for the high-volume strabismus surgeon and senior resident.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Rationale
sections.content: Adjustable suture surgery is a specialized technique where the final tension and position of a recessed or resected extraocular muscle (EOM) are modified in the immediate post-operative period (usually within 24 hours). This allows the surgeon to account for the 'unpredictable' brain-eye interface, including sensory fusion and muscle-contracture factors that static measurements cannot fully capture.

sections.title: Absolute & Relative Contraindications
content: Uncooperative patients (children or those with high anxiety/needle phobia)
Cognitive impairment (inability to follow instructions during adjustment)
Severe conjunctival scarring (precluding a clean sliding noose)
General anesthesia required for adjustment (rarely, unless propofol-assisted)
Extremely small-angle deviations where risks outweigh benefits
History of Malignant Hyperthermia or Suture Hypersensitivity

sections.title: Essential Surgical Instrumentation
content: 6-0 Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) on an S-29 or S-24 spatula needle
Fine-toothed forceps (0.12 or 0.3 Castroviejo)
Jameson or Green Muscle Hook
Suture-tying forceps (smooth)
Westcott scissors and Bishop-Harmon forceps
Caliper for precise limbal distance measurement
Silicone bolster or 'suture bridge' (optional)

sections.title: Surgical Technique: The 'Hang-back' Method
content: Step 1: Perform a limbal-based peritomy or fornix incision to expose the EOM.
Step 2: Secure the muscle with two locking 6-0 Vicryl sutures at the insertion.
Step 3: Disinsert the muscle from the globe.
Step 4: Pass the sutures through the original insertion or scleral tunnels (Hang-back technique).
Step 5: Create a 'Sliding Noose' using a separate short piece of 6-0 Vicryl around the long ends.
Step 6: Tie the muscle sutures in a temporary 'bow-tie' or pull them through the conjunctiva if utilizing a trans-conjunctival approach.

sections.title: The Post-Operative Adjustment Protocol
content: 1. Timing: Perform adjustment 4-24 hours post-op (once patient is alert).
2. Preparation: Instill 0.5% Proparacaine (topical anesthesia). Use Phenylephrine 2.5% for blanching if necessary.
3. Sensory Testing: Perform Cover-Uncover and Prism tests at distance and near.
4. Motor Testing: Assess ocular rotations and ensure no 'slipped muscle' sign.
5. Manipulation: If over-corrected, pull the long ends to advance the muscle. If under-corrected, use a hook to allow the muscle to recess further.
6. Final Tie-off: Once alignment is optimal, secure the permanent knot and trim the excess suture.

sections.title: Oculocardiac Reflex During Adjustment
content: Sudden Bradycardia (<60 bpm) during suture manipulation
Nausea/Vomiting/Syncope
Risk is higher with Medial Rectus tension
MANAGEMENT: Cease pulling immediately; monitor HR; apply cold compress to face if needed.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Aim for a slight overcorrection in Exotropia (Exo-drift is common).
Aim for orthophoria or trace esophoria in Esotropia.
In Thyroid Eye Disease, under-adjust slightly due to post-op inflammation increasing restriction.
Always perform a 'tug-test' before the patient leaves the OR to ensure the noose holds.
Use 'no-sting' lubricants post-adjustment to prevent suture-related discomfort.

sections.title: Potential Surgical Complications
content: Suture breakage during adjustment (Major Disaster)
Slipped muscle (Pseudo-palsy post-op)
Infection / Endophthalmitis (very rare, <1:1000)
Scleral perforation during tunnel creation
Chronic suture granuloma
Conjunctival scarring (Dellen formation)

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
sections.content: The PRISM (Prospective Randomized In-office Strabismus Management) Trial and works by Jampolsky (1970s) popularized this. Recent Cochrane reviews suggest that while it is highly effective in complex cases, it may not be necessary for routine primary horizontal strabismus in adults.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Innovations
content: Semi-adjustable techniques: Small adjustments via 'short-tag' sutures.
Minimally Invasive Strabismus Surgery (MISS) with adjustable loops.
Delayed adjustment (up to 7 days) using non-absorbable sutures and local lidocaine.
Use of Fibrin glue to secure conjunctiva over the adjustable site.
